verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains the three titles invoked for refuge as three independently sufficient sources of protection. A rabb manages, nurtures, and is resorted to for a person’s affairs, including averting threats; a king possesses prevailing authority to defend one; and an ilāh, especially one without partner, receives exclusive worship, so worshippers seek no other source, desire only what that god wills, and do only what he decrees. God alone is Lord, King, and God of humankind, as (39:6) states; His lordship and godhood are sufficient causes in (73:9), and His kingship in (57:5). Since the Prophet is among humankind, each title independently entails his seeking refuge with God; an editorial note adds that the command accordingly concerns all humankind.

The order moves from lordship, the nearest and most personal relation, to kingship, a more distant and general guardianship, to godhood, which is sought from sincere spiritual inclination rather than mere physical instinct. The absence of “and” shows that each attribute alone suffices to repel harm and that causality belongs exclusively to God in each dimension. Repeating al-nās rather than substituting pronouns likewise makes each title by itself a sufficient justification for recourse to Him.

Majmaʿ al-bayān defines waswās as the mind’s whispering voice, ḥadīth al-nafs. Al-Mizan apparently takes it here as an emphatic adjective; the author notes the grammatical debate over treating it instead as a maṣdar, while an editorial note says that reading would mean seeking refuge from the sneaky whisperings that penetrate souls. Khannās intensifies khunūs, “hiding after appearing”: Satan is so called because he tempts people, withdraws and waits when they remember God, then resumes when they become heedless. “Breasts” denotes the soul, the primary locus of cognition, because cognition is conventionally associated with the heart in the breast, as in (22:46). Finally, min is bayāniyyah, explanatory: the tempter is from among jinn and humankind, implying that some humans belong to the category of devils, as in (6:112).
